Metropolitan Museum of Art. Located on Fifth Avenue in New York City, the Metropolitan is one of the world's largest and most comprehensive art museums, spanning from ancient Egypt to contemporary work. Founded in 1870 and opened to the public in 1871, it was housed in a Beaux-Arts building designed by Richard Morris Hunt and has been expanded multiple times since, now spanning two city blocks. The museum holds over 1.7 million objects and epitomizes the American civic museum tradition. It houses the world's largest collection of American art, as well as major holdings of Egyptian, Greek, Roman, and Asian antiquities. The Temple of Dendur, an ancient Egyptian sandstone structure relocated to the museum in 1978, serves as both its architectural and curatorial centerpiece. Visitors encounter significant medieval arms and armor collection, including royal and knightly pieces, and the museum also has important costume and textile departments. Since its founding, the Met has offered nearly free admission through a pay-what-you-wish model for New York residents—a founding principle that has endured for over 150 years. The American Wing preserves furniture, decorative arts, and paintings that document United States cultural development from colonial times onward, making the Met a key node in American philanthropic and civic institutions. Its encyclopedic mission is exemplified by its Temple of Dendur and papyri collections, which reflect the Western museum's ambition to gather and preserve world history under one roof.
